## How the forecast works {#how}

We forecast all 35 Senate races on 3 November 2026 by combining synthetic voter responses with polling information. We sample 100 personas per state from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study, giving respondents with larger survey weights a greater chance of selection. Each persona receives nine news paragraphs, and four language models answer its voting question three times in their own words. We score these answers using Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR), then average the scores to estimate each state's Republican share of the two-candidate vote.

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. -->
Across the polled states, the models' synthetic Republican shares average about 5–9 percentage points above the polling estimates. Our headline method subtracts each model's average synthetic–poll gap before combining its estimate with the state's poll average. We call this bias correction, but the gap is measured against polls, not known election outcomes. Where polls are unavailable, we use the weighted 2024 CES vote share plus the average shift observed in polled states. The noisier of the two estimates gets less weight. This adapts the inverse-variance weighting of Lock and Gelman [@lockgelman2010], but our error estimates are approximate, and polls are not ground truth. We simulate 1,000 outcomes per model, allowing a shared national error to move states together, and give all four models equal weight. Adding the 65 seats not up for election produces a distribution over control of the 100-seat Senate. The [Discussion](#by-method) compares this combined forecast with synthetic-only and no-LLM alternatives.

## Methods {#methods}

The voting responses are synthetic; we did not conduct a new survey. We used Python 3.12 [@python] with pandas [@mckinney2010], NumPy [@harris2020], pyarrow [@arrow], matplotlib [@hunter2007], requests [@requests], lxml [@lxml] and tqdm [@tqdm], and sentence-transformers [@reimers2019] for the pilot embeddings; tests use pytest [@pytest] and pandera [@bantilan2020], and the website was built with Quarto [@quarto].

### Data {#data}

Our personas come from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study (CES), a survey of 60,000 US adults [@ces2024data; @ces2024guide]. Of these respondents, 38,307 lived in the 35 states holding Senate elections in 2026. Among them, 23,025 had a post-election voter-file weight, and 21,211 were validated as having voted in 2024. We used the post-election weight because the persona characteristics draw on both survey waves. Having a voter-file weight does not itself establish that someone voted, so we applied the validated-voter restriction separately.

We obtained candidate lists from Wikipedia on 21 October [@wikipedia2026]. Our two-candidate framework pairs the Republican with the leading Democratic or Independent opponent. Where several names were listed for a side, we used the candidate appearing most often in polls since 1 August. In Idaho, Nebraska and South Dakota, the opponent is Independent; in Montana, Independent Seth Bodnar polls ahead of Democrat Alani Bankhead. Additional candidates are acknowledged in the prompts but are not named individually.

We corrected Montana's candidate pair before the 31 October run. The 27 and 29 October runs had paired Republican Kurt Alme with Bankhead rather than Bodnar, so their synthetic estimates and matched polls described a different contest. Those earlier Montana results are not directly comparable with the final run.

Polling data come from PollResults, which compiles Senate polls originally tracked by The New York Times [@pollresults2026]. We use these data both in the combined forecast and as a benchmark for evaluating synthetic estimates. Polls are estimates of voter preferences, not election results; their role in setting the weights is discussed below.

### Personas

Each persona describes a respondent's age, education, race, gender, household income, ideology and party identification. Age is measured in 2024 and grouped as 18–29, 30–44, 45–64 or 65+. Education ranges from less than high school to a postgraduate degree. Race has five categories: White, Black, Hispanic, Asian and Other. Gender distinguishes men, women, non-binary respondents and other responses. Income retains the survey's 16 brackets and its “Prefer not to say” option. Ideology ranges from very liberal to very conservative, while party identification distinguishes strong, weak and leaning partisans from Independents. Uncertain responses are retained as “Not sure.” The models do not see the respondent's reported 2024 presidential vote, which we reserve for descriptive comparisons.

### Weighted sampling

We draw 100 personas in each state, with replacement, giving respondents with larger survey weights a greater chance of selection. Using replacement in every state keeps the procedure consistent, including in Wyoming and Alaska, whose eligible pools contain only 52 and 76 respondents. Across the sample, 904 of the 3,500 personas repeat someone already selected in the same state. About two-thirds of the selections in Alaska and Wyoming are repeats, so 100 personas do not mean 100 distinct people.

The survey weights enter when personas are drawn rather than when their answers are aggregated. In contrast, Wang et al. [-@wang2015] adjusted an opt-in Xbox sample after collecting responses, using multilevel regression and post-stratification. Our weighted draw reproduces each state's weighted CES composition in expectation, so each selected persona counts equally within its state. Applying the same survey weights again would double-weight the sample. This does not account for changes in the electorate between the 2024 presidential election and the 2026 midterms. Giving every state the same sample size supports separate race forecasts; pooled demographic comparisons require state-level weighting, as explained in [Crosstabs](#crosstabs).

### News summaries {#news}

We collect news from publisher RSS feeds and use Google News site searches when needed. Each collection covers the preceding 48 hours, removes duplicates and keeps up to 60 items per outlet. The ten outlets are The New York Times, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, USA Today, Fox News, New York Post, The Daily Wire, HuffPost, Mother Jones and Vox. Following Pew Research Center's audience and political-leaning information [@pew2025sources], we organise them into left-leaning outlets, newspapers and right-leaning outlets. “Newspapers” is a source group, not a claim of political neutrality.

GPT-4.1 Nano screens the titles and feed excerpts for US national significance and relevance to elections, policy, law or the economy, then writes a short paragraph for each retained item. The instructions exclude sports and other unrelated material and ask for a concrete development. Selected incorrect presidential and vice-presidential titles trigger a rewrite or exclusion. The resulting paragraphs are based on titles and excerpts rather than a full reading of each article; these checks do not independently verify the claims.

Each persona receives three randomly selected paragraphs from each source group, for nine in total. We join the existing paragraphs without asking a model to summarise them again. The same persona news block is used across models and repeat queries. A fixed random seed reproduces selections when the inputs are unchanged, and retries reuse the dated news selections. The tables below describe the retained pool, followed by one actual persona block chosen for illustration rather than at random.

{{< include data/03-results/comparison/news_summary.md >}}

### Prompts and models

We ask each persona how it would vote in its state's Senate race and randomise the order of the two candidates. We use models from four companies because their responses may differ systematically [@murray2026]. We record the model identifier returned by the provider and the query time, since a model can change even when its advertised name stays the same [@bisbee2024].

We use Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite through OpenRouter. Each model receives every persona’s prompt three times. We score the three responses separately and average their scores to reduce variation between individual answers. We ask for two or three sentences rather than percentages. We leave generation temperature at each provider's default and cap output at 800 tokens. Reasoning is disabled except for Gemini, which requires it and uses minimal effort. Empty, refused and otherwise invalid responses are counted and excluded from scoring rather than treated as zero support. Four Claude Haiku calls returned no answer in the 31 October run; the [cost table](#costs) reports calls and answers by model.

### Turning answers into voting probabilities {#scoring}

#### Why free-text answers?

LLM responses can concentrate too heavily on a small set of answers, a problem known as mode collapse. Heath and Alexander [-@heath2026] study whether free-text responses scored with Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR) better reproduce distributions in rating tasks. Maier et al. [-@maier2025] introduced SSR for purchase-intent ratings. We adopt the free-text approach for voting questions, while recognising that it does not by itself show that our responses avoid mode collapse.


#### Choosing the embedding model

On 26 October, we compared embedding models using 200 generated answers from Florida personas without news, 50 per voting model. Keyword rules identified 159 answers expressing a clear candidate choice. MiniLM placed 12 on the opposite side of the two-candidate scale; Gemini Embedding 2 misplaced one. The MiniLM errors were answers that supported Nixon but also mentioned Moody. Adding both names to each anchor made performance worse, so we retained single-candidate anchors and selected Gemini Embedding 2.

This was a limited diagnostic, not validation across all states. Neither setup captured indecision well: answers expressing it received an average weight of 0.14 on the middle category, while leaning and definite statements often received similar scores. These findings inform our choice of embedder but also show the limits of treating SSR weights as voting probabilities.


#### Semantic Similarity Rating

Gemini Embedding 2 represents each answer and five candidate-specific statements as numerical vectors. The statements express definite support for the Democratic or Independent candidate, leaning toward that candidate, being undecided or choosing another option, leaning Republican, and definite Republican support. Cosine similarity compares the direction of the answer's vector with each statement's vector, producing five similarity scores per answer.

We rescale those five scores to the range zero to one and apply softmax with a temperature of 0.25. Adding the first two weights gives support for the Democratic or Independent candidate; adding the final two gives Republican support. The middle weight represents other choices, indecision or nonvoting. Answers and statements are embedded in the same way, without separate query and document settings.

These allocations are not calibrated probabilities of an individual's actual vote. Vote choice is not an ordered rating scale, and the middle statement combines behaviours that may have different meanings. We do not apply a smoothing step or fit the temperature to voting outcomes, which we do not observe. This differs from the rating applications in Heath and Alexander [-@heath2026]. Softmax can distribute weight to both sides even when an answer names one candidate clearly; that is a property of the scoring rule, not evidence of greater variation between personas.


### Combining synthetic votes with polls {#combining}

We draw on Lock and Gelman's [-@lockgelman2010] inverse-variance approach to combining forecasts and polls. They estimate predictive uncertainty from past elections; we adapt the weighting idea to synthetic responses, using approximate error scales rather than reproducing their full Bayesian model.

We first average each persona's scores over repeated answers. The state's Republican two-candidate share is the mean Republican score divided by the sum of the mean scores for the two candidates. Resampling the personas 1,000 times gives a bootstrap measure of its variability. The outside estimate comes from information other than synthetic responses: the state polling average where available, or the weighted 2024 CES vote share plus the average shift in polled states (“2024 plus uniform swing”) otherwise. For the polling average, we use polls naming both selected candidates and ending within 45 days of the newest poll. We keep one question per poll, prefer likely-voter samples and average the two-candidate shares using sample-size weights.

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. -->
The combination has two steps. First, we subtract each model's average synthetic–poll gap across the polled states, giving the corrected share $m^*$. This assumes that polls are correct on average across those states; it does not establish that the original gap was a model error. Second, we average $m^*$ and the outside estimate $t$: the combined share is $c=(1-w)m^*+wt$, with outside weight $w=V_m/(V_m+V_t)$, so a larger synthetic variance gives the outside estimate more weight. The synthetic variance $V_m$ is the bootstrap variance plus a structural variance, estimated from the polled states as the across-state variance of the differences between corrected synthetic shares and polling averages, after subtracting the average bootstrap and polling variances. We apply a floor of $0.005^2$ to the structural variance so that it stays positive.

For polls, the error scale is sampling variance $p(1-p)/n$ plus an assumed $0.03^2$ for error beyond sampling [@shirani-mehr2018]. For states without polls, it comes from the errors around 2024 plus uniform swing. Draws are normal around the combined share with variance $1/(1/V_m+1/V_t)$, and a shared national error with standard deviation 0.03 is added. The correction assumes that each model's average synthetic–poll gap applies equally to every state, and the weights assume that synthetic and polling errors are independent, so they are approximations. The [Discussion](#by-method) compares the combination with synthetic-only and no-LLM forecasts, and with a version that keeps the bias and counts it as error instead.

### Sources of uncertainty {#uncertainty}

The simulations reflect persona resampling, the estimated structural synthetic error after the correction, uncertainty in polls or the historical benchmark, and a national error that moves states together. Pooling the four models also retains their disagreements. However, the average gap, variances and swing are estimated from the same polled states and treated as fixed, and we do not separately model regional errors or dependence between synthetic and polling errors. The [sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity) shows how changing the assumed national and polling errors affects control of the Senate.

### Tests

Before the full runs, we tested the workflow with five personas per state, free Laguna and Nemotron models, and a local MiniLM embedder. Separate test suites check the simulated data and the actual runs, using pytest and pandera. They check both individual tables and whether the sample, answers, scores and forecasts agree with one another.

We check that expected model–persona combinations and repeats are accounted for, failures are recorded, returned models match the requested provider, and token usage is available. Missing or refused answers must remain missing when scored. Valid scores must lie between zero and one and sum to one. Each forecast must assign valid vote shares and winners, fill all 100 Senate seats and keep the weighted estimate between its two inputs. A further check confirms that the combination uses the saved synthetic estimate and the recorded weights.

To check that the tests detect errors, we introduced missing probabilities, probabilities summing to 1.3, invalid vote-share totals and answers from another provider into a copy of the earlier data. Each was caught. Failed tests stop publication while preserving paid answers. These tests establish consistency of the calculations, not the accuracy of the election forecast.

### Design

We used election coverage from CNN, Politico, NPR, CBC and Reuters as design references [@cnn2024; @politico2024; @npr2024; @cbc2024; @reuters2024]. The website and figures share a colour palette, typography and table style so readers can compare results without relearning the presentation.

### Sensitivity to the assumed errors {#sensitivity}

Our headline forecast assumes a national error with a standard deviation of 3 percentage points and an additional polling error with a standard deviation of 3 percentage points, beyond sampling error. The national component moves states together within each simulation. The polling component affects the uncertainty and weight assigned to polling estimates. These are modelling assumptions, not known error sizes. The table varies both settings to show how much the probability of Republican control depends on them.

## Evaluation {#evaluation}

The forecast cannot be scored against the actual results until after the election on 3 November. Therefore, we compare it with a prediction market that forecasts the same races using a different method.

### Against a prediction market {#markets}

This comparison follows Wang et al. [-@wang2015], who compared their Xbox-based election forecasts with prediction markets before election results were available. We use PredictIt [@predictit2026], which has a market for each of the 35 races and for control of the Senate. It provides another forecast to compare with, rather than ground truth, and combines information through trading [@rothschild2009].

For each news day, we use the daily closing prices returned by PredictIt's API, rather than a live quote. A winning contract pays one dollar, so its price roughly reflects a probability. We normalise the two selected contract prices so that they sum to one: the Republican probability is its closing price divided by the sum of both prices. Third candidates are excluded to match our two-candidate framework. Montana is excluded from the state comparisons on 27 and 29 October because the saved prompts used Bankhead rather than Bodnar (see [Data](#data)); the Senate control comparison retains the full forecast for each day.

{{< include data/03-results/comparison/markets.md >}}

Points on the dashed line are races where the two agree; points in the shaded corners are races where they favour different sides. Hollow points are races with an independent instead of a Democrat; states that differ by 8 points or more are named.](figures/latest/market_comparison.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of 35 Senate races, our Republican winning probability against PredictIt's, with a 45-degree line and shaded corners where the two favour different sides."}

## API costs and time {#costs}

Each run uses 3,500 personas. Four models answer for each persona three times, giving 42,000 calls per run. We calculate costs from the recorded token counts using OpenRouter’s list prices as of 25 October. Answer embeddings cost about US$0.50 per run, and news screening costs less than US$0.10. The total estimated cost is about US$9 per run. OpenRouter charged about US$7.20 per run because DeepSeek’s off-peak prices were lower. The total project bill was US$41.38, including the test run and a repeated run. The README lists the charges by day.

{{< include data/03-results/comparison/costs.md >}}

## Discussion {#discussion}

### Comparing synthetic-only, combined and no-LLM forecasts {#by-method}

The table compares four methods using the latest run's saved inputs. Synthetic-only uses the original SSR shares without polling adjustment. The combined forecast—the headline result—removes each model's average gap from the polls and averages the corrected shares with state polling averages where available. In states without usable polls, it instead combines them with the 2024 CES vote share shifted by the average change observed in polled states (“2024 plus uniform swing”). The third version combines the raw synthetic shares with the outside estimates. It also uses the mean squared synthetic–poll gap in the error scale, rather than the variance of the remaining differences after correction. This changes both the input shares and their weights; it is not a comparison that holds the weights fixed. The no-LLM benchmark uses the same polling averages and 2024-plus-swing estimates, but excludes synthetic responses. This comparison shows how adding synthetic responses changes the forecast; it does not establish which method is more accurate before election results are available.

### Do synthetic voters reproduce partisan voting patterns? {#fidelity}

Argyle et al. [-@argyle2023] describe algorithmic fidelity as a model's ability to reproduce patterns of human responses across groups. We compare Republican support across demographic and party-identification groups: the synthetic responses for the 2026 Senate races alongside the same personas' reported Republican vote in the 2024 presidential election. Their earlier vote was not included in the prompts. This asks whether the models reproduce earlier partisan patterns, rather than whether they correctly predict each person's next vote. Some Senate opponents are Independents, so non-Republican support cannot always be labelled Democratic support.

Bisbee et al. [-@bisbee2024] caution that aggregate resemblance can coexist with overly uniform responses and distorted relationships between characteristics and opinions. The [Crosstabs table](#crosstabs) compares synthetic Republican support with reported 2024 Republican voting across these groups. Comparing party-identification groups helps show whether the models treat party as too decisive, while groups without a clear party preference provide a harder check. Close agreement with the 2024 column is not enough: turnout, candidates and voter preferences can change between elections. We therefore treat these tables as a description of the synthetic sample, not as evidence that its forecast is correct.

### Free text and Semantic Similarity Rating {#ssr-discussion}

SSR scores do not always match the strength of support expressed in an answer [@heath2026; @maier2025]. Even when a response clearly chooses one candidate, the scoring rule can assign some support to the other. This can make a group appear less partisan without making the personas' answers more diverse. Our limited embedding check also found that undecided answers were not clearly distinguished from candidate support. The forecast therefore depends partly on how we define the reference statements and choose the softmax temperature, rather than only on what the models say.

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. -->
### The news the personas read

Murray and Alexander [-@murray2026] find that party identification in a persona can limit the effect of news on its answers. Our [news comparison](#synthetic) shows relatively small changes in the average synthetic share across the recorded runs, although individual states move by different amounts. Every prompt states the persona's party identification, which may help explain this stability. Because model answers also vary between runs, we cannot attribute the observed changes entirely to news exposure or conclude that news has no effect on real voters.

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. -->
### Uncertainty and the correlation between states

The [sensitivity table](#sensitivity) shows that our assumptions about error affect which party is likely to control the Senate. If polls miss support for one party across the country, several states where the candidates are closely matched could change winners together [@gelman2020]. Errors could also be concentrated in one region, which our shared national error does not fully capture. Although our forecasts change little across the three days, the wide seat intervals show that many outcomes remain possible. A stable forecast is not necessarily an accurate one.

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. -->
### What agreement with the market tells us

The [market comparison](#markets) shows that our forecast and PredictIt often agree. However, much of the high correlation may come from races where one candidate is already strongly favoured. Disagreements matter more where the candidates are closely matched and where a few seats could change control of the Senate. Traders can read the same polls used in our combined forecast, so agreement does not provide an independent check of those polls. Prices can also be affected by low trading activity and how traders value unlikely outcomes [@rothschild2009; @wang2015]. The comparison is useful, but it cannot tell us which forecast is more accurate before the election results are available.

### Limitations {#limitations}

We do not have results from past elections to check how far this synthetic forecasting method typically misses the outcome. Unlike Lock and Gelman [-@lockgelman2010], we therefore use approximate error estimates rather than estimates based on historical forecast performance. We use polls as a benchmark, but they can miss voters who do not respond, misjudge who will vote, or become outdated as preferences change. The headline forecast subtracts each model's average synthetic–poll gap, so a shared polling error could also affect the corrected synthetic estimates. The comparison without bias correction keeps that gap and gives synthetic estimates less weight. As the [method comparison](#by-method) shows, both the input shares and the weighting rules affect the result; neither version is known to be more accurate.

Our uncertainty estimates also rely on assumptions. As described in [Sources of uncertainty](#uncertainty), we treat estimated error sizes as fixed and do not capture every way that errors may be related. This may make the seat intervals too narrow. The additional polling error has an assumed standard deviation of 3 percentage points, rather than a value established for these races; the sensitivity table also considers 2 and 4 points. Combining polls from one aggregator does not remove errors they may share [@shirani-mehr2018]. Repeated selections of the same CES respondent are also treated as separate personas in the bootstrap. This may understate uncertainty, especially in Alaska and Wyoming, where the original respondent pools are small.

In the 10 states without usable polls, the outside estimate is the 2024 CES vote share plus uniform swing. Applying the same shift to every state does not account for the appeal of individual Senate candidates. Synthetic estimates may also misrepresent how demographic characteristics and party identification translate into a candidate choice. In Kentucky, for example, many personas identify as Democrats but describe themselves as conservative. The resulting synthetic support should not be assumed to measure those voters' actual support for the Senate candidates.

Our forecast considers only two candidates in each race. Other candidates, indecision and nonvoting are not fully represented in the final two-candidate shares. Montana makes this limitation clear: we compare Republican Kurt Alme with Independent Seth Bodnar and leave out Democrat Alani Bankhead. The forecast cannot show how support would be divided among all three candidates or how that division could affect the winner. The scoring limitations are discussed under [Free text and Semantic Similarity Rating](#ssr-discussion).

Even with saved prompts, provider defaults and model updates can change the answers obtained in a rerun. We also collected news on only three days, so these runs tell us little about how synthetic responses would react to a wider range of events. Future work could vary the amount and mix of news while holding other inputs constant.

To improve the method, we would need comparable forecasts from more elections to test the correction and weights. We could then investigate whether error sizes differ by region or by how closely matched the candidates are, whether the four models should receive different weights, and whether estimating uncertainty across several dates gives more reliable results.

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. -->
### Conclusion: what the synthetic voters add {#conclusion}

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. Numbers from the 31 October run. -->
Synthetic-only strongly favours Republican control, while both the combined forecast and the no-LLM benchmark favour the Democratic caucus. Synthetic responses change the forecast relative to the no-LLM benchmark, but they receive a small share of the combined weight. This project therefore demonstrates a way to incorporate silicon sampling into an election forecast, rather than establishing that it improves on polling and historical information. When election results are available, vote-share comparisons must use the same denominator: the votes for the two selected candidates, rather than all candidates. Winner comparisons must also acknowledge that an omitted candidate could win or affect the outcome, especially in Montana. Broader evidence would require evaluation across more elections and settings.
